segments.text: It's 7.38 a.m. on April 18, 1942, in the storm-tossed Western Pacific.
Pitching through 30-foot swells is the aircraft carrier USS Hornet,
and chained to her soaked flight deck is something that shouldn't exist at sea.
16 twin-engine U.S. Army B-25 Mitchell land bombers,
loaded with high explosives for a surprise revenge strike on Tokyo.
In command, Lieutenant Colonel Jimmy Doolittle still has 10 hours before reaching his launch point.
Then, through the spray, a lookout freezes at his binoculars.
Surface vessel ahead! 20,000 yards! Turn to starboard!
Bobbing 11 miles away is the number.
23. Nito Maru
A 70-ton Japanese picket boat stationed offshore to spot American warships.
Immediately, the light cruiser USS Nashville breaks formation and opens fire,
her 6-inch guns thundering across the gale.
Inside the rocking wheelhouse, the Japanese crew knows they have minutes to live,
and lunges for the radio.
Send the alert! Enemy carriers sighted! Warn headquarters immediately!
Disappearing between 30-foot waves, the tiny boat is maddeningly hard to hit.
It takes the rolling cruiser up to 938 rounds of 6-inch shells to finally blow the Nito Maru apart.
By then, Navy radio interceptors know the worst.
Tokyo got the message.
On the Hornets' bridge, Vice Admiral William Bull Halsey faces a brutal choice.
America only has a handful of carriers left in the Pacific.
Steaming 200 miles closer toward an alerted Japan
could lead the Hornet and her escort carrier, the USS Enterprise, straight into an ambush.
Either they shove 16 army bombers overboard and run,
or Doolittle launches right now, 10 hours early and 200 miles farther out than his fuel math allows.
Neither man hesitates.
Over the loudspeakers blares the call that seals 80 men's fates.
Army pilots! Man your planes!
To see why launching this far out borders on suicide, look at the physics trap America faced
after Pearl Harbor.
Washington desperately needed to hit Tokyo to shatter the myth of Japanese invincibility.
Yet U.S. Navy carrier bombers could only strike targets 250 miles away,
while Japan guarded its coast with land bombers able to sink ships 600 miles out to sea.
To survive, a carrier had to launch long-range army bombers outside Japan's reach and send them west
to friendly airfields in China, because landing a heavy bomber back onto a short carrier deck
without a tailhook was physically impossible.
It had to be a one-way trip.
Enter the North American B-25B Mitchell.
On paper, putting 16 on a carrier looked insane.
With a rigid wingspan of 67 feet 7 inches, the B-25 couldn't fold its wings,
couldn't fit down the Hornet's elevators, and normally needed 1,500 feet of concrete runway to lift off.
Jammed onto the Hornet, Doolittle's lead bomber had just 467 feet of wet steel deck
before a 60-foot drop into the Pacific.
Solving that equation took Jimmy Doolittle, a daredevil racing pilot
who also held one of America's first doctorates in aeronautical engineering from MIT.
At a secret Florida strip, Doolittle's team stripped every spare pound of metal off the B-25.
Out came the heavy lower gun turret, long-range radios, and steel armor.
Out came the top-secret Norden bombsite,
replaced by a simple aiming sight Captain Ross Greening built from 20 cents' worth of scrap aluminum,
dubbed the Mark Twain.
And to guard the undefended tail without adding weight,
Greening added a brilliant bluff.
Two wooden broomsticks, painted flat black,
and poked through the rear plexiglass to look like twin .50 caliber machine guns.
Every pound saved went straight into gasoline.
Mechanics nearly doubled fuel capacity from 646 gallons to 1,141 gallons,
strapping a collapsible 160-gallon rubber bladder above the bomb bay,
stuffing a flexible tank into the crawlway,
and stacking 10 5-gallon gas cans inside the fuselage to pour in mid-flight.
Even then, launching 200 miles early pushed their fuel reserve below zero.
At 8.20am, Doolittle sits at the controls of plane number one.
No B-25 has ever launched from a carrier before.
Keeping his left tires glued to a painted white stripe
clears the Hornet's steel island tower by less than 6 feet.
Veer right by a yard,
and 31,000 pounds of gas and bombs explode on deck.
Doolittle has just one aerodynamic edge.
With the Hornet steaming full speed into a gale,
over 45 miles per hour of wind is already rushing across his wings before his wheels move.
At the bow, the launch officer times the rise of the hull with a checkered flag
and whips it down.
Doolittle releases the brakes and firewalls his twin 1,700-horsepower right cyclone engines.
Hurtling down the white stripe,
his right wingtip slices past the steel bridge,
and just as the Hornet's bow heaves upward on a wave,
Doolittle lifts clear into the sky with feet to spare.
Fifteen overloaded bombers follow him into the spray.
Last in line is plane number 16,
Bat Out of Hell,
piloted by First Lieutenant Billy Farrow.
As Farrow edges forward,
fierce prop wash rocks his bomber across the slick deck,
and a navy deckhand slips into a spinning propeller,
losing his arm.
Seconds later,
Bombardier Corporal Jacob de Schaeser
spots a jagged foot-wide hole
smashed straight through their plexiglass nose.
Reporting the damage means scrubbing his flight and shoving his plane overboard.
Knowing the hole will add drag and burn extra fuel,
Farrow still jams the throttles forward,
dips below the bow,
and claws into the sky.
Four hours later,
as Japan's coast looms ahead,
the bombers drop to 50 feet above the waves.
Every crew braces for gunfire.
After all,
the Nittomaru warned Tokyo at dawn,
All hands,
stand by for heavy fire at the beach.
They blast across the shoreline at 200 miles per hour,
and nothing happens.
Below them,
towns sit quiet in clear sunshine.
Unknowingly,
the raiders have hit two blind spots in Japan's defences.
First,
Imperial Naval Headquarters received the dawn warning,
and fell into a math trap.
Assuming US carriers only carried short-range navy planes,
Japanese commanders calculated the Americans would have to steam closer all day
and strike the next morning,
April 19th.
Nobody imagined army land bombers launching 750 miles out.
Second,
Tokyo had just wrapped up a morning air raid drill.
When olive drab bombers roar over the suburbs at noon,
civilians look up and wave,
assuming they're part of the exercise.
Suddenly,
Doolittle's co-pilot,
2nd Lieutenant Richard Cole,
shouts,
9 fighters,
up high!
Doolittle hugs the rooftops as 9 Japanese fighters cruise overhead,
flying right past without recognizing an American bomber over their own capital.
Crossing the Sumida River,
Doolittle skirts the Imperial Palace,
strictly off-limits so America doesn't turn the Emperor into a martyr,
and climbs to 1,200 feet over Tokyo's northern factory district.
With no autopilot on the 20-cent Mark Twain site,
Doolittle holds speed and altitude steady by hand,
while Bombardier Staff Sergeant Fred Bremer lines up a military arsenal.
Hold her steady,
Hold her steady, Chief!
Bremer hits the release.
Four 500-pound clusters burst open,
scattering 512 4-pound magnesium thermite bomblets across the target.
Burning at 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit,
they punch through wooden roofs and ignite towering fires that jolt Tokyo awake.
Sirens wail,
Flak fills the sky with black smoke,
and Doolittle dives to treetop height,
weaving safely out of the city.
Minutes behind him,
Tokyo is waiting for plane number 10,
piloted by 1st Lieutenant Richard Joyce.
Before takeoff,
Doolittle and his men had wired pre-war Japanese friendship medals onto several 500-pound bombs,
returning Tokyo's peace tokens with high explosives.
As Joyce blasts a major steel mill,
Flak erupts around him.
A shell explodes yards away,
ripping an 8-inch shrapnel hole through the rear fuselage
and showering turret gunner Staff Sergeant Edwin Horton with metal fragments.
Horton, you alright back there?
Still in one piece?
Keep moving!
As enemy fighters dive to cut him off,
Joyce shoves the nose into a 300-mile-per-hour power dive
and outruns them to the coast.
Near Yokohama,
Captain Ross Greening in plane number 11,
the Harikariya,
can't avoid a fight.
Four Japanese fighters jump his lone bomber right above the trees.
Now Greening's bluff faces the ultimate test.
Swooping behind his undefended tail,
Japanese pilots spot two black barrels jutting from the rear plexiglass.
Greening's painted broomsticks!
Hesitating to fly into what looked like twin .50 calibers,
the fighters arc higher to attack from above,
putting themselves dead into the sights of Sergeant Melvin Gardner's real upper turret.
Gardner hammers out .50 calibre incendiary bursts
that send two fighters plunging in smoke,
while Greening bombs an oil refinery,
the blast slamming both pilots' heads against the cockpit roof,
and escapes so low he flies underneath high-voltage power lines.
Further south over Nagoya,
Billy Farrow's bat-out-of-hell,
wind and flak smoke howling through its broken nose,
sets an oil depot and the Mitsubishi aircraft plant ablaze.
Incredibly, not a single B-25 is shot down over Japan.
Yet, over the East China Sea, cold math catches up.
Crewmen pour the last five-gallon cans into the tanks,
puncture the tins so they'll sink,
and toss them overboard.
While plane number 8,
burning extra gas from faulty carburetors,
diverts north to land in the Soviet Union near Vladivostok,
navigator George Barr checks the numbers for the rest.
15 bombers will run dry over open ocean,
more than 100 miles short of China.
Then, halfway across the sea,
Doolittle's navigator Hank Potter shouts,
Colonel, the wind just shifted behind us!
A freak storm front has kicked up a 25-mile-per-hour tailwind,
pushing 15 dying bombers just far enough to reach the Chinese coast.
Yet that same storm swallows them in pitch-black rain and fog over jagged mountains.
Doolittle calls the friendly airfield at Chuqiao for the radio homing beacon meant to guide them down.
Chuqiao station!
American bomber calling!
Do you copy?
Dead static.
Due to secrecy delays and the early launch,
the beacon isn't on.
Blind over unseen peaks with empty tanks,
Doolittle gives the only order left.
Bail out!
Across eastern China,
airmen leap into the howling night.
Doolittle lands deep in a muddy, fertilized rice paddy that cushions his injured ankle,
convinced losing every plane will earn him a court-martial.
Instead, brave Chinese villagers and guerrillas rescue 64 raiders,
smuggling them to safety.
Two crews run out of luck.
First Lieutenant Dean Hallmark's plane number 6 ditches in the surf,
drowning two men while three survivors wash ashore into Japanese hands.
Inland, Billy Farrow pushes Bat Out of Hell west through the storm,
only to bail out with dry tanks over Japanese-occupied Nanchang.
Those eight captured raiders endure months of torture and a sham trial in Shanghai.
On October 15, 1942,
Billy Farrow, his gunner Harold Spatz,
and Dean Hallmark are tied to crosses and executed by firing squad,
while First Lieutenant Robert Meader dies of starvation in prison,
leaving four captives to survive until 1945.
Worse still, Japan unleashes a four-month reprisal across eastern China,
killing up to 250,000 Chinese civilians for sheltering the Americans.
Yet strategically, those 16 stripped-down bombers changed the war.
16 tons of bombs barely scratched Japan's industry,
but hitting Tokyo in broad daylight humiliated Japan's high command.
Back home, America erupted in hope,
and Doolittle received the Medal of Honor.
In Tokyo, shamed commanders pulled frontline fighters back to guard the homeland,
and immediately approved Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto's risky gamble
to trap America's carriers at Midway.
Seven weeks after lifting off 467 feet of pitching deck
with 20-cent sights and painted broomsticks,
Doolittle's raid lured the Japanese fleet
straight into an American ambush at Midway,
sending four Japanese aircraft carriers to the bottom in a single day,
and turning the tide of the Pacific War forever.
